# Prompt caching writes on every gate call and is never read across calls: the marked prefix is not stable

## Observed — measured, with a control

Two `rebar review-plan` runs executed BACK TO BACK, seconds apart, well inside the ~5-minute
cache TTL, on two DIFFERENT tickets (1c39 then 9baf), with REBAR_USAGE_LOG capturing every call.
All calls on Bedrock via the project default. Per-call figures:

    pass                                RUN A in / write        RUN B in / write        RUN B read
    plan-reviewer (frontier/opus)        5286 / 2800             5394 / 2908             0
    plan-review-prerequisite-verifier    3809 / 1545             3872 / 1608             0
    plan-review-verifier                 7136 / 4871             7199 / 4934             0
    plan-review-coach                    1999 / 0                2062 / 0                0
    ticket-digest (trivial/haiku)        2131 / 0                2816 / 0                0
    TOTALS                               write 9216, read 0      write 9450, read 0

RUN B WROTE THE CACHE AGAIN INSTEAD OF READING IT. Every read is zero in both runs.

## The mechanism this points at

Each pass's cache-WRITE size tracks its input size almost exactly across the two runs
(plan-reviewer 5286 -> 5394 input, 2800 -> 2908 write; verifier 7136 -> 7199 input,
4871 -> 4934 write). A cache prefix that were genuinely stable would produce the SAME marked
prefix and therefore a hit on the second run. That the write grows in step with per-ticket input
says the MARKED PREFIX ITSELF VARIES PER CALL — i.e. per-ticket content is landing ahead of the
cache breakpoint, so the cache key is unique every time and can never be reused.

`capabilities.cache_settings_for` marks the INSTRUCTIONS plus tool definitions, and
`structured_run.estimate_marked_prefix_tokens` derives the marked size from the SYSTEM PROMPT. So
the hypothesis to test first is that the rendered system prompt/instructions embed per-ticket
material (the plan text, the ticket digest, or similar) rather than being invariant across runs.

## What is NOT the explanation — ruled out by evidence

* NOT "caching is off on Bedrock". Three of five passes write thousands of tokens per run, so the
  settings are emitted and the provider accepts them.
* NOT "the read path is broken". Intra-CALL reuse demonstrably works: the production review bot's
  multi-step agentic records read large caches within a single call — e.g. a code-review pass with
  steps=9/125 logged cache_read=386204 against in=430479, and another with steps=17/125 logged
  cache_read=493547. Those are steps 2..N reusing what step 1 wrote inside one conversation.
* NOT the sub-minimum-prefix condition for the three writing passes. That condition explains the
  two passes that write ZERO — coach (whole prompt small) and ticket-digest, where the diagnostic
  fired verbatim: "only 477 tokens sit ahead of the cache breakpoint, below this model's
  4096-token minimum, while 8634 of the 9111 billed input tokens ride AFTER it unmarked". It does
  not explain a pass that writes 4871 tokens and then never reads them.

## Why it costs money rather than being merely untidy

A cache write is billed at a PREMIUM over ordinary input; a read is billed at a steep discount.
The current behaviour pays the premium on every gate call and collects the discount only within a
single multi-step call. For single-step passes — which is every pass in a plan review, all five
records show requests=1 — the write is pure loss: nothing ever reads it. Every plan review on this
project pays roughly 9,000-11,000 premium-rate cache-write tokens for zero benefit.

## Scope

- `src/rebar/llm/capabilities.py` `cache_settings_for` — where the breakpoints are placed.
- `src/rebar/llm/structured_run.py` `estimate_marked_prefix_tokens` and the ineffective-cache
  diagnostic — the estimate is the instrument that would have caught this and did not.
- whatever renders the plan-review system prompt / instructions, if that is where per-ticket
  content is crossing the breakpoint.

## Approach — investigate before changing anything

The first task is NOT a fix, it is to identify precisely which bytes sit ahead of the breakpoint
and whether they vary per run. Capture the rendered system prompt for the same pass on two
different tickets and diff them; the varying region is the defect's location. Only then decide
whether the fix is to move per-ticket content behind the breakpoint (into the user message) or to
split the instructions into an invariant prefix and a per-run suffix.

Do NOT "fix" this by disabling caching on single-step passes: that trades a real, measurable
premium for giving up the cross-call discount entirely, and the cross-call discount is the larger
prize once the prefix is stable. Note also that the existing diagnostic's advice — "the changeable
thing is where the breakpoint sits, not the size of the prompt" — is exactly right here and was
never triggered for the writing passes, so consider whether the predicate should also flag
"wrote every call, never read".

## Testing

- an oracle that renders the same pass's marked prefix for two different tickets and asserts they
  are BYTE-IDENTICAL. This is the RED test: it should fail today. Verify RED before any fix.
- a live two-run oracle (the experiment above) asserting cache_read > 0 on the second run for at
  least the frontier pass, run inside the TTL.
- a guard that the ineffective-cache diagnostic fires when a pass writes on every call and never
  reads, so this class cannot recur silently.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [x] the bytes that vary ahead of the cache breakpoint are identified and cited, with a diff of
      the rendered marked prefix for one pass across two different tickets.
- [x] the marked prefix for a given pass is byte-identical across tickets, pinned by a test
      verified RED against today's behaviour.
- [x] a second run of the same pass inside the cache TTL records cache_read > 0, evidenced by an
      actual usage-log capture rather than by inspection.
- [x] the diagnostic in `structured_run` also flags the write-every-call-never-read shape, so a
      regression is loud.
- [x] the cost change is stated with figures — premium-rate write tokens per review before and
      after — so the benefit is measured rather than asserted.
